items.title: Intro to HTML - What HTML Is
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn what HTML is, what it does, and how you write and save it before you create your first page.

items.title: What is HTML?
items.text:
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.

  • HyperText refers to text that can link to other text. A HyperText page can point to another page through links.
  • Markup means that you mark up plain text with labels which describe what each part is.
  • Language means that HTML provides a fixed set of labels, called tags, which every browser understands.

HTML is not a programming language. It has no logic, no variables, and no if statements. It is a markup language because it describes the structure and meaning of content.

items.title: What does HTML do?
items.text:
HTML tells the browser what things are, not what they look like.

<h1>Bakery</h1>
<p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
  • The line <h1>Bakery</h1> means that the text is the main title of the page.
  • The line <p>Fresh bread daily.</p> means that the text is a paragraph.

The browser then decides how to display that meaning with a large bold title and a plain paragraph. The exact colours, fonts, and layout are added later with CSS. Behaviour and interactivity are added later with JavaScript.

Technology Job Example HTML Structure and meaning "This is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a link." CSS Looks and layout "Make the heading red and centred." JavaScript Behaviour "When clicked, show the menu."

This course covers HTML only. One core rule applies throughout the course: choose tags by meaning, never by looks.

items.title: Tags vs elements
items.text:
Beginners often mix up these two terms, but they describe different things:

  • A tag is the label inside angle brackets, for example <p>, </p>, or <h1>.
  • An element is the complete unit, which consists of the opening tag, the content, and the closing tag.
An opening tag A closing tag

Most elements have both an opening tag and a closing tag:

<h1>Bakery</h1>      <!-- opening <h1>, text, closing </h1> -->
<p>Fresh bread.</p>  <!-- opening <p>, text, closing </p> -->

A few elements have no content and no closing tag. These elements are called void (empty) elements:

<br>   <!-- line break -->
<hr>   <!-- horizontal rule -->
<img src="bread.jpg" alt="Loaf of bread">  <!-- image -->

items.title: Attributes
items.text:
Attributes provide additional information about the contents of an element. They appear on the opening tag of the element and they consist of two parts, a name and a value, which are separated by an equals sign.

HTML Attributes

The pattern to notice

Opening tags can carry extra information in the form of attributes, such as src and alt in the example above. Closing tags never carry attributes. You will meet each attribute in its own chapter, so for now it is enough to recognise the general shape.

items.title: How HTML is stored, written, and saved
items.text:
1. HTML is plain text. No special software creates it. It consists of ordinary characters stored in a file.
  2. You write HTML in a text editor such as VS Code, Notepad, or TextEdit, which are all programs that save plain text. Do not use Word or Google Docs because they add hidden formatting which breaks HTML.
  3. You save the file with an .html ending, for example index.html. The .html ending tells the operating system and the browser that the file should be read as a webpage.
  4. You open the file in a browser by double-clicking it or by dragging it into Chrome, Firefox, or Edge. The browser reads the file from top to bottom and draws the page.

Practical rules for this course:

  • Save every exercise as index.html inside its own folder.
  • Always use UTF-8 encoding, which is the default in most editors. UTF-8 keeps characters such as é, ñ, and ü intact.
  • Name files in lowercase without spaces, for example index.html instead of My Page.HTML.
  • After every change, save the file and then refresh the browser. If you do not save, the change will not appear on the screen.

You do not need a server, the internet, or any build tool yet. A text file and a browser provide the complete setup.

items.title: Try it: your first 3 lines
items.text:
1. Open your editor and create a new file.
  2. Type exactly this:
<h1>Bakery</h1>
<p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
  1. Save the file as index.html.
  2. Open the file in a browser.

You have just written HTML with two elements, four tags, one title, and one paragraph. Every later chapter introduces more labels for more kinds of content.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Idea Detail What HTML is HyperText Markup Language, a set of labels for structure and meaning What it does It states what content is; the browser renders it, CSS controls looks, and JS controls behaviour Tag The bracketed label, for example <p> or </p> Element The complete unit, which is the opening tag plus the content plus the closing tag, or a lone void element such as <br> How it lives A plain-text .html file which is written in a code editor and opened in a browser

items.text:
1. Read the chapters in order, because each chapter builds on the previous one.
  2. Type out every example in a file called index.html and open that file in a browser.
  3. Chapters marked reference contain full detail, so skim them on the first pass and return to them when you need the exact syntax.

items.title: 01 - Basic Structure of an HTML Page
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn the skeleton on which every webpage is built, starting with the declaration, then the single root element, then the metadata, and finally the visible content.

items.title: The full template
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Your Page Title</title>
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Your page content -->
</body>
</html>

Copy this template at the start of every page. Read it from top to bottom, because the order is significant.

items.title: <!DOCTYPE html> - declaration
items.text:
• This line declares the document as HTML5 so that browsers render the page in standards mode instead of quirks mode.
  • It is not a tag, so it has no closing tag and no attributes. It must always be the very first line, with nothing above it.
<!DOCTYPE html>

items.title: <html> - root element
items.text:
• The html element is the parent of everything. It wraps both <head> and <body>, and its closing tag </html> must be the last line of the file.
  • The lang attribute sets the page language, which screen readers and search engines use:
<html lang="en">
lang value Meaning en English sw Swahili fr French

items.title: <head> - invisible metadata
items.text:
• The head element holds setup information which the visitor never sees on the page itself, including <title>, <meta charset>, <meta viewport>, <link> to CSS, and <script> to JS.
  • It is the first child of <html>, and it always appears before <body>.
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Bakery</title>
</head>
Tag inside <head> Job <title> The tab and window title, which is also used as the search-result title <meta charset="utf-8"> The character encoding, which should always be included <meta name="viewport" …> The instruction which makes mobile browsers scale the page correctly, and which should always be included

items.title: <body> - visible content
items.text:
• Everything the visitor sees belongs in the body, including headings, paragraphs, lists, images, links, and divs.
  • It is the second child of <html>, and each page contains exactly one <body> element.
<body>
  <h1>Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
</body>
The struture of an HTML page

items.title: Hierarchy (who is inside who)
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>      declaration,comes first, owns nothing
<html>               PARENT,wraps all
  <head>             1st child,invisible setup
  <body>             2nd child,all visible content
  • The <html> element is the parent, while <head> and <body> are its children.
  • The <head> element always appears before the <body> element. No visible content ever belongs in <head>, although the <title> appears on the browser tab.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Each page contains one <!DOCTYPE>, one <html>, one <head>, and one <body>, with no additional copies.
  • Close the tags in reverse order, so the <html> tag which opens second also closes last.
  • If you omit <meta charset>, non-English characters can display incorrectly. If you omit the viewport tag, the layout breaks on mobile phones.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Order Tag Role 1st <!DOCTYPE html> Declaration 2nd <html lang> Root parent 3rd <head> Invisible metadata 4th <body> Visible content

items.title: 02 - What Are Headings?
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn what headings are for before you meet all six levels.

items.title: Headings = the document outline
items.text:
Headings are section titles. Together they form the outline of the page, in the same way that chapter titles outline a book:

<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
  • The <h1> element holds the main title of the page, and each page contains exactly one h1 element.
  • The <h2> element marks major sections, while <h3> through <h6> mark progressively smaller subsections.

items.title: Meaning First -  size second
items.text:
Browsers draw <h1> as the largest heading and <h6> as the smallest, with bold text by default. However, you should never select a heading for its size:

  • If you need small text, use CSS instead of <h4>.
  • If you need large text, use CSS instead of <h1>.
  • Select the level which describes the position of the section in the outline.

items.title: Why headings matter beyond looks
items.text:
• Screen readers: Blind users jump from heading to heading in order to navigate. When you skip from h1 to h3, they encounter a missing level and lose their place.
  • Search engines: The text in h1 and h2 elements carries extra weight when the search engine decides what the page is about.
  • Skimmers: Most visitors scan the headings before they read any paragraph text.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
1. Use exactly one <h1> element per page.
  2. Never skip a level, for example from h1 to h3 or from h2 to h4.
  3. Keep headings short and descriptive.
  4. Do not use a heading to style text which is not really a heading.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Idea Detail What Section titles which form the page outline Levels h1 for the main title through h6 for the deepest subsection Pick by Meaning and position, never visual size Matters for Readers, screen readers, and search engines

items.title: 03 - Headings h1–h6 Showcase
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will meet all six heading levels and see how their relative sizes compare.

items.title: The rule first
items.text: Each page must contain one <h1> element. Heading levels must never be skipped, for example from level 1 to level 3.

items.title: All six levels
items.text: Tag Renders (approx.) Use for <h1> Bakery Homepage (largest) Page title, used once <h2> Our Menu Major sections <h3> Drinks Subsections <h4> Hot Drinks Sub-subsections <h5> Tea Notes Deep detail <h6> Fine print head (smallest) Rarely used, deepest level

items.title: Snippets
items.text:
<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
<h3>Drinks</h3>
<h4>Hot Drinks</h4>
<h5>Tea Notes</h5>
<h6>Fine print head</h6>

The following example shows correct nesting, and you can see that no level has been skipped:

<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
<h3>Drinks</h3>
<h2>Prices</h2>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• If a page contains two <h1> tags, split the page into two pages or demote one of the titles to <h2>.
  • If an <h1> element is followed directly by an <h3> element, insert the missing <h2> element, even when it feels redundant.
  • A paragraph which has been styled to look large is not a heading, so screen readers will not list it as one.
Headings

items.title: Recap
items.text: Level Size hint Role h1 Biggest Page title, used once h2 Large Sections h3–h6 Shrinking Subsections, never skipped

items.title: 04 - What Are Paragraphs?
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn how paragraphs work as blocks of thought, and how br and hr differ from paragraphs.

items.title: Paragraphs = blocks of thought
items.text:
A paragraph groups sentences into one block which expresses one idea. It is the default unit of web text:

<p>Fresh bread baked every morning.</p>
  • Block-level: Each <p> element starts on a new line, and browsers add space above and below it automatically.
  • Readability: Each <p> element should hold one idea. Short paragraphs scan far better on screens than long walls of text.

items.title: <p> vs <br>
items.text:
• The <p> element starts a new thought, which means it creates a new block.
  • The <br> element creates a line break inside the same thought, which is useful for an address, a poem, or a signature block:
<p>Line one<br>Line two, same thought</p>
Paragraphs

Never stack several <br> tags such as <br><br><br> in order to fake paragraph spacing. The <p> element, together with CSS margins, exists for that purpose, while stacked breaks carry no meaning for screen readers.

items.title: <hr> = thematic break
items.text:
The <hr> element marks a scene change between blocks, for example when a story moves to a new scene or when a menu switches to prices:

<p>Menu</p>
<hr>
<p>Prices</p>

It renders as a horizontal line, but its meaning is that the topic shifts at this point, so it is not decoration.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
1. Place one idea in each <p> element and keep paragraphs short.
  2. The <br> element is an empty tag without a closing tag, and it should be used sparingly.
  3. The <hr> element is an empty tag which signals a shift in topic, not a decorative divider.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Meaning Empty? p Block of thought No br Line break within the same thought Yes hr Thematic break Yes

items.title: 05 - Paragraphs, Breaks, Rules (Syntax)
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn the exact syntax for p, br, and hr.

items.title: <p> - paragraph
items.text:
The p element defines a block of thought. The space above and below each paragraph is added automatically:

<p>Fresh bread baked daily.</p>

items.title: <br> - line break
items.text:
The br element is an empty tag, so it has no closing tag. It breaks the line inside the same paragraph:

<p>Line one<br>Line two</p>

It renders as:

Line one Line two

items.title: <hr> - thematic break
items.text:
The hr element is an empty tag, so it has no closing tag. It signals a shift in topic between blocks:

<p>Menu</p>
<hr>
<p>Prices</p>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• A <br> element inside a heading is occasionally acceptable, for example in a two-line title, but it must never be used for vertical spacing, because that spacing is the job of CSS.
  • Multiple <hr> elements in a row almost always indicate that the sections need headings instead.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Closing tag? Job p Yes, </p> Block of thought br No Line break within the same thought hr No Thematic break

items.title: 06 - Combined: Headings + Paragraphs in the Basic Structure
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will see where text lives inside the skeleton introduced in Chapter 01.

items.title: The same skeleton - now with text
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Bakery</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
</body>
</html>

items.title: Where each piece lives
items.text:
• The <h1> and <p> elements live inside the <body> element, because they are visible content.
  • The <head> element holds only the <title> element in this example, and it never holds visible text, although the title itself appears on the browser tab.
  • The <html> element is the parent of both sections, while <!DOCTYPE html> is the declaration above them all.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text:
• Text which is placed in <head> outside the <title> element will not render, and this mistake is a classic beginner bug.
  • Every chapter from here on adds tags which live in <body>, except for page-level setup tags.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Zone Holds Visible? <head> <title>, <meta> No, tab title only <body> h1–h6, p, and everything from Ch. 07 onward Yes

items.title: 07 - Meaning vs Looks (The Core Rule)
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn the most important distinction in HTML text, which is that semantic elements describe meaning while visual elements only change appearance.

items.title: The rule
items.text:
When in doubt, go semantic. Use <strong> instead of <b>, and use <em> instead of <i>.

Semantic elements tell browsers, screen readers, and search engines what the text means. Visual elements only change the rendering.

items.title: <strong> - importance
items.text:
The strong element renders as bold text, and screen readers announce it as important. It also carries SEO weight:

<p>Warning: <strong>Do not enter.</strong></p>

items.title: <b> - visual bold only
items.text:
The b element looks bold, but it means nothing to assistive technology or to search engines:

<p>Use <b>bold</b> for looks alone.</p>

You should prefer <strong> unless you explicitly mean styling only, for example when you mark a product name inside a review.

items.title: <em> - emphasis
items.text:
The em element renders as italic text, and screen readers stress it when they read it aloud:

<p>We are <em>closed</em> today.</p>

items.title: <i> - visual italic only
items.text:
<p>The term <i>croissant</i> is French.</p>

Typical legitimate uses of i include foreign words, technical terms, and transliterations. When you want to place stress on a word, use <em> instead.

items.title: <mark> - highlighted passage
items.text:
The mark element marks text as relevant, in the same way a highlighter pen marks paper, and it shows a yellow background by default:

<p>Result: <mark>passed</mark></p>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Nesting is acceptable, for example <strong><em>both</em></strong>, provided that you close the tags in reverse order.
  • The <b> and <i> elements are not deprecated. They are simply free of meaning, so they should be used rarely and deliberately.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Meaning? Renders strong Important Bold b None Bold em Emphasis Italic i None Italic mark Relevant or highlighted Highlighted

items.title: 08 - Code Family
items.text: HTML provides elements for displaying computer code, programming examples, and technical text on a webpage.

items.title: 1. Inline Code
items.text:
The <code> element is used for a short piece of code within a sentence.

<p>
    Use the <code>print()</code> function to display text in Python.
</p>

The browser normally displays <code> text using a monospace font.

items.title: 2. Code Blocks
items.text:
For multiple lines of code, <pre> is commonly used together with <code>.

<pre><code>
name = "Jonathan"
print(name)
</code></pre>

<pre> preserves spaces and line breaks in the content.

items.title: 3. Preserving Formatting with <pre>
items.text:
The <pre> element displays text using the spacing and line breaks written in the HTML.

<pre>
Name: Jonathan
Age: 27
Country: Uganda
</pre>

The spaces and line breaks are preserved.

items.title: 4. Code with HTML
items.text:
When displaying HTML code on a webpage, remember that the browser normally interprets HTML tags instead of displaying them.

For example:

<p>Hello World</p>

To display the tags as text, you need to use HTML character references:

<pre><code>
<p>Hello World</p>
</code></pre>

The browser displays:

<p>Hello World</p>

items.title: 5. Keyboard Input
items.text:
The <kbd> element represents keyboard input.

<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save the file.</p>

It is useful when writing instructions involving keyboard shortcuts.

items.title: 6. Program Output
items.text:
The <samp> element represents sample output from a computer program.

<p>
    The program returned:
    <samp>Hello, World!</samp>
</p>

items.title: 7. Variables
items.text:
The <var> element represents a variable in mathematical or programming expressions.

<p>The area of a rectangle is <var>width</var> × <var>height</var>.</p>

items.title: Important Elements
items.text: Element Purpose <code> Represents computer code <pre> Preserves spaces and line breaks <kbd> Represents keyboard input <samp> Represents program output <var> Represents a variable

items.title: Goal
items.text: In this chapter, you will learn about small HTML elements that add meaning to text. These elements help browsers, search engines, screen readers, and other tools understand what the content represents.

items.title: <abbr> - Abbreviation
items.text:
The <abbr> element represents an abbreviation or acronym.

<p>I am learning <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>.</p>

The title attribute provides the full meaning of the abbreviation.

When the user hovers over the abbreviation, browsers commonly display the value of title.

Another example:

<p>
    The <abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr>
    provides health information around the world.
</p>

items.title: <time> - Date and Time
items.text:
The <time> element represents a specific date, time, or period.

<p>The class starts at <time>9:00 AM</time>.</p>

For a date:

<p>The event is on <time>2026-10-07</time>.</p>

The datetime attribute can provide a machine-readable version of the date or time.

<p>
    PyCon Africa starts on
    <time datetime="2026-10-07">October 7, 2026</time>.
</p>

The text is written for humans, while datetime gives computers a standard format to understand.

items.title: <del> - Deleted Text
items.text:
The <del> element represents text that has been removed or deleted.

<p>
    The price is <del>50,000</del> 40,000 shillings.
</p>

Browsers normally display deleted text with a line through it.

items.title: <ins> - Inserted Text
items.text:
The <ins> element represents text that has been added or inserted.

<p>
    The price is <del>50,000</del> <ins>40,000</ins> shillings.
</p>

This can be useful when showing changes to a document.

items.title: <sub> - Subscript
items.text:
The <sub> element displays text below the normal text line.

It is commonly used in chemical formulas.

<p>Water is H<sub>2</sub>O.</p>

It can also be used in mathematical expressions:

<p>x<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub></p>

items.title: <sup> - Superscript
items.text:
The <sup> element displays text above the normal text line.

It is commonly used for powers and mathematical expressions.

<p>2<sup>3</sup> = 8</p>

It can also be used for ordinal numbers:

<p>1<sup>st</sup> place</p>

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Element Meaning <abbr> Abbreviation or acronym <time> Date or time <del> Deleted content <ins> Inserted content <sub> Subscript <sup> Superscript

These elements may look small, but they give HTML semantic meaning rather than simply changing how text looks.

items.title: 1. Inline Quotes
items.text:
The <q> element is used for a short quotation within a sentence.

<p>
    Albert Einstein said, <q>Imagination is more important than knowledge.</q>
</p>

Browsers normally display quotation marks around the text.

items.title: 2. Block Quotes
items.text:
The <blockquote> element is used for a longer quotation that stands on its own.

<blockquote>
    The important thing is not to stop questioning.
    Curiosity has its own reason for existing.
</blockquote>

The browser normally displays a block quotation with indentation.

items.title: 3. Citing the Source
items.text:
The cite attribute can be used with <blockquote> to specify the source of a quotation.

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/article">
    The important thing is not to stop questioning.
</blockquote>

The cite attribute provides the source information but is not normally displayed on the page.

items.title: 4. The <cite> Element
items.text:
The <cite> element is used to identify the title of a work, such as a book, movie, song, or article.

<p>
    My favourite book is <cite>Things Fall Apart</cite>.
</p>

It can also be used when identifying the source of a quotation:

<blockquote>
    The world is a fine place and worth fighting for.
</blockquote>

<p>
    Source: <cite>Ernest Hemingway</cite>
</p>

items.title: 5. <q> vs <blockquote>
items.text: Element Purpose <q> Short, inline quotation <blockquote> Longer, separate quotation <cite> Identifies the title or source of a work cite attribute Specifies the URL of the source

items.title: Example
items.text:
<p>
    She said, <q>Learning never stops.</q>
</p>

<blockquote>
    Education is the most powerful weapon which you can use
    to change the world.
</blockquote>

items.title: 11 - Special Blocks
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn three block tags for exact whitespace, contact information, and fine print.

items.title: <pre> - preformatted text
items.text:
The pre element keeps spaces and line breaks exactly as you type them, and it is the only element which behaves this way. It is the home of multi-line code:

<pre>line 1
  indented line 2</pre>

Pair the pre element with the <code> element when you want a code block which also carries meaning:

<pre><code>def hello():
    print("hi")</code></pre>

items.title: <address> - contact info
items.text:
The address element holds contact information for the author or owner of the page or section, and it must not be used for any postal address which happens to appear in the text:

<address>hello@mhsm.web<br>Dar es Salaam</address>

Browsers usually render this element in italic. It belongs near the footer or the author bio.

items.title: <small> - fine print
items.text:
The small element holds side comments such as copyright lines, disclaimers, legal notes, and attributions:

<small>© 2026 MHSM. All rights reserved.</small>

Browsers render it one step smaller than normal text. It does not make the text unimportant, since it only marks the text as secondary.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Inside a <pre> element, you must still escape < as <, because otherwise the browser reads it as a tag.
  • The <address> element must not contain headings or sectioning content, so restrict it to contact lines.
  • A <small> element inside a <footer> element is the classic pattern for a copyright line.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Job Watch out pre Exact whitespace Escape < as < address Author or owner contact Not any address small Fine print Still readable, not hidden

items.title: 1. What are Links?
items.text:
Links allow users to move from one webpage or location to another.

HTML uses the <a> element, also called the anchor element, to create links.

<a href="about.html">About Us</a>

The text About Us is what the user clicks.

items.title: 2. The <a> Element
items.text:
The <a> element creates a hyperlink.

<a href="https://www.google.com">Google</a>

The link has:

  • <a>: the anchor element
  • href: specifies where the link goes
  • Google: the clickable text

items.title: 3. The href Attribute
items.text:
The href attribute specifies the destination of the link.

<a href="about.html">About Us</a>

The destination can be:

  • Another webpage
  • Another page in the same website
  • A different website
  • A specific location on the same page
  • An email address

items.title: 4. Linking to Another Website
items.text:
You can create a link to an external website using its URL.

<a href="https://www.wikipedia.org">Wikipedia</a>

Another example:

<a href="https://www.python.org">Python</a>

items.title: 5. Linking to Another Page
items.text:
You can link to another HTML page in your website.

Suppose you have:

website/
├── index.html
├── about.html
└── contact.html

From index.html, you can link to about.html:

<a href="about.html">About Us</a>

And to contact.html:

<a href="contact.html">Contact Us</a>

items.title: 6. Linking to a Page in a Folder
items.text:
If the page is inside a folder, include the folder in the path.

website/
├── index.html
└── pages/
    ├── about.html
    └── contact.html

<a href="pages/about.html">About Us</a>

items.title: 7. Opening a Link in a New Tab
items.text:
The target attribute can specify where the linked page should open.

<a href="https://www.python.org" target="_blank">
    Python
</a>

target="_blank" tells the browser to open the link in a new browsing context, commonly a new tab.

items.title: 8. Linking to an Email Address
items.text:
The mailto: scheme can be used to create an email link.

<a href="mailto:example@email.com">
    Send me an email
</a>

Clicking the link can open the user's email application.

items.title: 9. Linking to a Specific Location on a Page
items.text:
You can link to a particular section of the same page using an id.

First, give an element an id:

<h2 id="contact">Contact Us</h2>

Then create a link to it:

<a href="#contact">Go to Contact Us</a>

The # tells the browser to look for an element with that id.

items.title: 10. Linking an Image
items.text:
An image can also be used as a link.

<a href="about.html">
    <img src="images/logo.png" alt="About Us" width="200">
</a>

When the user clicks the image, they are taken to about.html.

items.title: 11. Navigation Links
items.text:
Links are commonly used to create website navigation.

<nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="about.html">About</a>
    <a href="services.html">Services</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

Navigation links help users move between the different pages of a website.

items.title: 12. Complete Example
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>My Website</title>
</head>

<body>

    <h1>My Website</h1>

    <nav>
        <a href="index.html">Home</a>
        <a href="about.html">About</a>
        <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
    </nav>

    <h2>Welcome</h2>

    <p>
        Visit the
        <a href="https://www.python.org">Python website</a>
        to learn more about Python.
    </p>

</body>
</html>

items.title: Important Elements and Attributes
items.text: Element/Attribute Purpose <a> Creates a link href Specifies the link destination target Specifies where the link should open target="_blank" Opens the link in a new browsing context mailto: Creates an email link #id Links to a specific location on a page

items.title: 1. What are Images?
items.text:
Images are pictures displayed on a webpage. They can make webpages more attractive and help communicate information.

HTML uses the <img> element to display images.

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

items.title: 2. The <img> Element
items.text:
The <img> element is used to display an image.

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A beautiful landscape">

The <img> element does not have a closing tag.

items.title: 3. The src Attribute
items.text:
The src attribute specifies the location of the image.

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

If the image is inside a folder:

<img src="images/cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

The image can also come from a URL:

<img src="https://example.com/cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

items.title: 4. The alt Attribute
items.text:
The alt attribute provides a description of the image.

<img src="dog.jpg" alt="A brown dog">

The alt text is useful when:

  • The image cannot be displayed.
  • Someone uses a screen reader.
  • The image needs to be described to someone who cannot see it.

items.title: 5. Image Width and Height
items.text:
The width attribute controls the width of an image.

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat" width="400">

The height attribute controls the height.

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat" width="400" height="300">

Both attributes can be used together.

items.title: 6. Images in Folders
items.text:
Images are often stored in a separate folder.

website/
├── index.html
└── images/
    ├── cat.jpg
    └── dog.jpg

To display cat.jpg:

<img src="images/cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

items.title: 7. Image Captions
items.text:
A caption is visible text that describes or identifies an image.

HTML provides <figure> and <figcaption> for images with captions.

<figure>
    <img src="cat.jpg" alt="A sleeping cat">
    <figcaption>A cat sleeping on a chair.</figcaption>
</figure>

items.title: <figure>
items.text: Groups an image and its caption together.

items.title: <figcaption>
items.text: Contains the visible caption.

items.title: 8. alt Text vs Caption
items.text:
alt text and captions have different purposes.

<figure>
    <img src="elephant.jpg" alt="An elephant walking through grass">
    <figcaption>An elephant in Queen Elizabeth National Park.</figcaption>
</figure>

alt

Provides a description of the image, mainly for accessibility and when the image cannot be displayed.

figcaption

Provides a visible caption that appears with the image.

items.title: 9. Complete Example
items.text:
<figure>
    <img
        src="images/mountain.jpg"
        alt="A mountain surrounded by trees"
        width="500"
    >

    <figcaption>
        A mountain surrounded by trees.
    </figcaption>
</figure>

items.title: Important attributes and elements
items.text: Element/Attribute Purpose <img> Displays an image src Specifies the image location alt Describes the image width Sets the image width height Sets the image height <figure> Groups an image with related content <figcaption> Adds a visible image caption

items.title: 14 - Lists
items.text: Goal: In this chapter you will learn how to structure related items with unordered, ordered, and description lists.

items.title: <ul> - unordered list
items.text:
The ul element defines a bulleted list in which the order of the items does not matter. Each item is an <li> element:

<ul>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
</ul>

items.title: <ol> - ordered list
items.text:
The ol element defines a numbered list in which the order matters, for example for steps or rankings. Browsers number the items automatically:

<ol>
  <li>Mix flour and water.</li>
  <li>Knead ten minutes.</li>
  <li>Bake at 220°C.</li>
</ol>

Start the numbering elsewhere with the start attribute, or reverse it with the reversed attribute:

<ol start="5">
  <li>Fifth step first</li>
</ol>

items.title: Nesting lists
items.text:
An <li> element can hold a complete sub-list. The nested list goes inside the <li> element, not after it:

<ul>
  <li>Bread
    <ul>
      <li>White</li>
      <li>Brown</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Milk</li>
</ul>

items.title: <dl> - description list
items.text:
The dl element defines term and definition pairs, which are useful for glossaries, menus with descriptions, and metadata:

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>HyperText Markup Language,page structure.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Cascading Style Sheets,page styling.</dd>
</dl>
Tag Job dl The whole description list dt Term dd Definition or description

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Only an <li> element may be a direct child of ul or ol, so do not place bare text or <p> wrappers at that level.
  • Do not fake lists with <br> tags or - dashes, because readers then lose the count and the structure.
  • Navigation menus are lists too, and you will meet the <nav><ul>… pattern constantly.

items.title: Recap
items.text: List Use when Markers ul Order is irrelevant Bullets ol Order matters Numbers, added automatically dl Term leads to definition None

items.title: 15 - Tables
items.text: Goal: In this chapter, you will learn how to use HTML tables to organize related information into rows and columns. You will learn how to create tables, add headings and data, group rows, and add captions.

items.title: What is an HTML Table?
items.text:
An HTML table is used to present information in rows and columns.

Tables are useful for information such as:

  • Student marks
  • Product prices
  • Class timetables
  • Employee information
  • Sales records
  • Schedules

For example:

Name Age Class John 15 S2 Sarah 14 S1 David 16 S3

In HTML, this information can be represented using several elements.

items.title: The Basic Table
items.text:
The <table> element creates a table.

<table>
</table>

However, an empty table does not contain any information. We need to add rows and cells.

A simple table looks like this:

<table>
    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
        <td>14</td>
        <td>S1</td>
    </tr>
</table>

items.title: <tr> - Table Row
items.text:
The <tr> element creates a table row.

<tr>
</tr>

Each <tr> represents one horizontal row in the table.

For example:

<table>
    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
        <td>14</td>
    </tr>
</table>

This creates two rows.

John     15
Sarah    14

items.title: <td> - Table Data Cell
items.text:
The <td> element represents a cell containing table data.

td means table data.

<td>John</td>

A row can contain multiple data cells:

<tr>
    <td>John</td>
    <td>15</td>
    <td>S2</td>
</tr>

This row has three cells.

| John | 15 | S2 |

items.title: <th> - Table Header Cell
items.text:
The <th> element represents a heading for a row or column.

th means table header.

Instead of:

<tr>
    <td>Name</td>
    <td>Age</td>
    <td>Class</td>
</tr>

use:

<tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Age</th>
    <th>Class</th>
</tr>

A complete table might look like:

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Class</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
        <td>14</td>
        <td>S1</td>
    </tr>
</table>

The first row contains the column headings.

items.title: <caption> - Table Caption
items.text:
The <caption> element gives a table a title or description.

<table>
    <caption>Student Information</caption>

    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Class</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

The caption describes what the table is about.

A <caption> should be placed immediately after the opening <table> tag.

items.title: <thead> - Table Header
items.text:
The <thead> element groups the rows containing the table's header information.

<table>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Name</th>
            <th>Age</th>
            <th>Class</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

</table>

It is particularly useful for larger or more structured tables.

items.title: <tbody> - Table Body
items.text:
The <tbody> element groups the main data rows of a table.

<table>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Name</th>
            <th>Age</th>
            <th>Class</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>John</td>
            <td>15</td>
            <td>S2</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Sarah</td>
            <td>14</td>
            <td>S1</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

</table>

The <tbody> contains the main information in the table.

items.title: <tfoot> - Table Footer
items.text:
The <tfoot> element groups rows containing summary or footer information.

For example, a sales table might contain a total:

<table>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Product</th>
            <th>Price</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>Bread</td>
            <td>5,000</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Milk</td>
            <td>3,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <th>Total</th>
            <th>8,000</th>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>

</table>

items.title: Complete Table Structure
items.text:
A well-structured table can contain:

<table>
    <caption>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>
            <th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>
            <td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <td>
            <td>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>

</table>

A complete example:

<table>

    <caption>Student Marks</caption>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Name</th>
            <th>Mathematics</th>
            <th>English</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>John</td>
            <td>85</td>
            <td>78</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Sarah</td>
            <td>92</td>
            <td>88</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

</table>

items.title: Understanding Rows and Columns
items.text:
Consider this table:

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Class</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

The table has 2 rows and 3 columns.

             Columns
          ↓       ↓       ↓

       | Name | Age | Class |
       |------|-----|-------|
Rows → | John | 15  | S2    |

A <tr> creates a row.

A <th> or <td> creates a cell within that row.

items.title: Combining Cells
items.text: HTML allows cells to span multiple rows or columns.

items.title: colspan
items.text:
The colspan attribute allows a cell to span multiple columns.

<table>
    <tr>
        <th colspan="2">Student Information</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

The header cell spans two columns.

items.title: rowspan
items.text:
The rowspan attribute allows a cell to span multiple rows.

<table>
    <tr>
        <th rowspan="2">Name</th>
        <td>John</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
    </tr>
</table>

The Name cell spans two rows.

items.title: Tables Are for Tabular Data
items.text:
Tables should be used when information has a meaningful relationship between rows and columns.

Good examples include:

Student | Class | Mark
Product | Price | Quantity
Date    | Event | Location

Tables should not be used simply to position elements on a webpage. Page layout should be handled using modern HTML and CSS.

items.title: Important Elements and Attributes
items.text: Element/Attribute Purpose <table> Creates a table <caption> Gives the table a title or description <tr> Creates a table row <th> Creates a header cell <td> Creates a data cell <thead> Groups table header rows <tbody> Groups the main table rows <tfoot> Groups footer or summary rows colspan Makes a cell span multiple columns rowspan Makes a cell span multiple rows

items.title: Recap
items.text:
The basic table structure is:

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>Heading</th>
        <th>Heading</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Data</td>
        <td>Data</td>
    </tr>
</table>

For a more structured table:

<table>

    <caption>Table Title</caption>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Heading</th>
            <th>Heading</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>Data</td>
            <td>Data</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <td>Summary</td>
            <td>Total</td>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>

</table>

The key idea is:

<table> → <tr> → <th> / <td>

A table contains rows, and each row contains cells.

items.title: 16 - Forms Basics
items.text: Goal: In this chapter, you will learn how to create forms that allow users to enter and submit information. You will learn how forms work, how to create different types of inputs, how to label fields, and how to group related form controls.

items.title: What is an HTML Form?
items.text:
An HTML form is a section of a webpage where users can enter or select information.

Forms are commonly used for:

  • Login pages
  • Registration
  • Contact forms
  • Search boxes
  • Surveys
  • Feedback
  • Ordering products
  • Booking services

A simple form might look like this:

<form>
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name">

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

items.title: <form> - Form Container
items.text:
The <form> element defines a form.

<form>

    <!-- Form controls go here -->

</form>

The elements used to collect information are placed inside the <form>.

A form can contain:

  • <input>
  • <label>
  • <textarea>
  • <select>
  • <option>
  • <button>
  • <fieldset>
  • <legend>

items.title: <label> - Describing a Form Control
items.text:
The <label> element provides a description for a form control.

<label for="name">Name:</label>
<input type="text" id="name">

The for attribute of the label should match the id of the input.

for="name"
     ↓
id="name"

This connects the label to the input.

Clicking the label can also focus the associated input.

items.title: <input> - User Input
items.text:
The <input> element is used to collect many different types of information.

<input type="text">

The type attribute determines what kind of input the browser should provide.

Some common types are:

Type Purpose text General text email Email address password Password number Number date Date time Time checkbox Multiple choices radio One choice from a group file File upload search Search input submit Form submission

items.title: Text Input
items.text:
The text type is used for general text.

<label for="name">Name:</label>
<input type="text" id="name">

For example, a user could enter:

Jonathan

items.title: Email Input
items.text:
The email type is intended for email addresses.

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email">

Browsers can provide appropriate validation and input behavior for email addresses.

items.title: Password Input
items.text:
The password type is used for passwords.

<label for="password">Password:</label>
<input type="password" id="password">

The characters entered are normally hidden from view.

items.title: Number Input
items.text:
The number type is used for numerical values.

<label for="age">Age:</label>
<input type="number" id="age">

You can also specify a minimum and maximum value:

<input type="number" id="age" min="10" max="100">

items.title: Date Input
items.text:
The date type allows the user to select a date.

<label for="birthday">Date of Birth:</label>
<input type="date" id="birthday">

The browser may provide a date picker.

items.title: Time Input
items.text:
The time type allows the user to select a time.

<label for="appointment">Appointment Time:</label>
<input type="time" id="appointment">

items.title: Textarea
items.text:
The <textarea> element is used when the user needs to enter multiple lines of text.

<label for="message">Message:</label>

<textarea id="message"></textarea>

Unlike <input>, <textarea> has an opening and closing tag.

You can specify its initial size using rows and cols:

<textarea id="message" rows="5" cols="40"></textarea>

items.title: Select and Option
items.text:
The <select> element creates a drop-down list.

The <option> element defines the choices.

<label for="country">Country:</label>

<select id="country">
    <option>Uganda</option>
    <option>Kenya</option>
    <option>Tanzania</option>
    <option>Rwanda</option>
</select>

The user can select one of the available options.

items.title: Radio Buttons
items.text:
Radio buttons allow the user to select one option from a group.

<p>Gender:</p>

<input type="radio" id="male" name="gender" value="male">
<label for="male">Male</label>

<input type="radio" id="female" name="gender" value="female">
<label for="female">Female</label>

The important part is that the radio buttons have the same name:

name="gender"

This tells the browser that they belong to the same group.

items.title: Checkboxes
items.text:
Checkboxes allow users to select multiple options.

<p>Languages you know:</p>

<input type="checkbox" id="python" name="language" value="python">
<label for="python">Python</label>

<input type="checkbox" id="javascript" name="language" value="javascript">
<label for="javascript">JavaScript</label>

<input type="checkbox" id="java" name="language" value="java">
<label for="java">Java</label>

Unlike radio buttons, multiple checkboxes can be selected.

items.title: The name Attribute
items.text:
The name attribute gives a form control a name that can be used when the form data is submitted.

<input type="text" name="username">

For example:

<label for="username">Username:</label>
<input type="text" id="username" name="username">

Here:

  • id identifies the element within the HTML document.
  • name identifies the field when form data is submitted.

items.title: The value Attribute
items.text:
The value attribute specifies the value associated with a form control.

<input
    type="radio"
    id="uganda"
    name="country"
    value="uganda"
>
<label for="uganda">Uganda</label>

If the user selects this option, its value is:

uganda

items.title: Required Fields
items.text:
The required attribute tells the browser that a field must be completed before the form can be submitted.

<label for="email">Email:</label>

<input
    type="email"
    id="email"
    name="email"
    required
>

The browser will prevent submission if the required field has not been completed.

items.title: Placeholder Text
items.text:
The placeholder attribute provides a temporary hint inside an input.

<input
    type="text"
    id="username"
    name="username"
    placeholder="Enter your username"
>

The placeholder disappears when the user starts entering information.

A placeholder should not replace a proper <label>.

items.title: The Submit Button
items.text:
A form usually needs a button that allows the user to submit the information.

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

The type="submit" tells the browser that the button submits the form.

items.title: The <button> Element
items.text:
The <button> element creates a clickable button.

<button>Click Me</button>

For forms, it is good practice to explicitly specify the button type:

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

A button can also be used for other actions, such as:

<button type="button">Click Me</button>

items.title: Form Submission
items.text:
The <form> element can use action to specify where the form data should be sent.

<form action="/register">
    ...
</form>

The method attribute specifies how the browser should submit the data.

Two commonly used methods are:

<form action="/register" method="post">
    ...
</form>

and:

<form action="/search" method="get">
    ...
</form>

items.title: GET
items.text:
GET is commonly used when requesting or searching for information.

The submitted values can appear in the URL.

items.title: POST
items.text:
POST is commonly used when submitting information that changes or creates data.

The submitted values are sent in the request body.

items.title: Complete Example
items.text:
<form action="/register" method="post">

    <h2>Create an Account</h2>

    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input
        type="text"
        id="name"
        name="name"
        required
    >

    <br>

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input
        type="email"
        id="email"
        name="email"
        required
    >

    <br>

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input
        type="password"
        id="password"
        name="password"
        required
    >

    <br>

    <label for="country">Country:</label>

    <select id="country" name="country">
        <option value="uganda">Uganda</option>
        <option value="kenya">Kenya</option>
        <option value="tanzania">Tanzania</option>
    </select>

    <br>

    <label for="message">About You:</label>

    <textarea
        id="message"
        name="message"
        rows="5"
        cols="40"
    ></textarea>

    <br>

    <button type="submit">Register</button>

</form>

items.title: Grouping Form Controls
items.text:
The <fieldset> element groups related form controls together.

The <legend> element provides a title for the group.

<fieldset>

    <legend>Personal Information</legend>

    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email">

</fieldset>

This is particularly useful for larger forms.

items.title: Important Elements and Attributes
items.text: Element/Attribute Purpose <form> Defines a form <label> Describes a form control <input> Creates an input control <textarea> Creates a multi-line text input <select> Creates a drop-down list <option> Creates an option in a select list <button> Creates a button <fieldset> Groups related form controls <legend> Describes a fieldset type Specifies the type of input or button id Identifies an element name Names a form field for submission value Specifies the value submitted for a control required Makes a field required placeholder Provides a temporary input hint action Specifies where form data is submitted method Specifies how form data is submitted

items.title: Recap
items.text:
The basic structure of a form is:

<form>

    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>

</form>

The most important relationship to remember is:

<form>
    ├── <label>
    ├── <input>
    ├── <textarea>
    ├── <select>
    │     └── <option>
    └── <button>
</form>

A form provides the structure for collecting information. HTML defines the fields and their meaning, while a server-side application can receive and process the submitted data.

items.title: 17 - Grouping: div, section, span
items.text: Goal: In this chapter, you will learn how to group HTML content using <div>, <section>, and <span>. Although these elements can all be used to group content, they have different meanings and purposes.

items.title: Why Group Content?
items.text:
As webpages become larger, we need ways to organize related content.

For example, a page might contain:

Header
    Navigation

Main content
    About us
    Our services

Footer

HTML provides different elements for grouping these parts of a webpage.

items.title: <div> - Generic Block Container
items.text:
The <div> element is a generic container for grouping content.

<div>
    <h2>About Us</h2>
    <p>We build software for businesses.</p>
</div>

<div> does not tell the browser what the content means.

It simply says:

These elements belong together as a group.

This makes <div> useful when there is no more meaningful semantic element that describes the content.

items.title: <div> as a Container
items.text:
A <div> can contain many different elements.

<div>
    <h2>Student Information</h2>

    <p>Name: Jonathan</p>
    <p>Class: S2</p>

    <a href="profile.html">View Profile</a>
</div>

The <div> groups all of this content together.

It is commonly used when working with CSS and JavaScript because it provides a convenient element to target.

items.title: <section> - A Thematic Section
items.text:
The <section> element represents a thematically related section of content.

<section>
    <h2>About Us</h2>

    <p>
        We teach students how to build websites.
    </p>
</section>

Unlike <div>, <section> has semantic meaning.

It tells browsers and other tools:

This is a distinct section of the document.

items.title: Sections Usually Have a Heading
items.text:
A section will commonly have a heading that describes its content.

<section>
    <h2>Our Services</h2>

    <p>We provide web development services.</p>
</section>

Another section can follow it:

<section>
    <h2>Contact Us</h2>

    <p>Get in touch with our team.</p>
</section>

The headings help users and assistive technologies understand the structure of the page.

items.title: <div> vs <section>
items.text:
Consider:

<div>
    <h2>About Us</h2>
    <p>We teach programming.</p>
</div>

and:

<section>
    <h2>About Us</h2>
    <p>We teach programming.</p>
</section>

Both can group the content, but they communicate different things.

items.title: <div>
items.text:
Means:

This content is grouped together.

items.title: <section>
items.text:
Means:

This is a distinct section of related content.

Use <section> when the content represents a meaningful section of the document.

Use <div> when you simply need a generic container and there is no more appropriate semantic element.

items.title: <span> - Generic Inline Container
items.text:
The <span> element is a generic container for small pieces of inline content.

<p>
    My favourite language is
    <span>Python</span>.
</p>

Unlike <div>, <span> does not create a new block.

It stays within the surrounding text.

For example:

<p>Hello <span>Jonathan</span>, welcome!</p>

The <span> is part of the same paragraph.

items.title: <span> for Part of a Sentence
items.text:
A common use of <span> is to identify a particular part of some text.

<p>
    The weather today is
    <span>very warm</span>.
</p>

The <span> does not give the text any special semantic meaning by itself.

It simply provides a way to identify that particular piece of content.

items.title: <span> vs <div>
items.text: The main difference is how they participate in the page's flow.

items.title: <div>
items.text:
A block-level container.

<div>
    First group
</div>

<div>
    Second group
</div>

The groups normally appear on separate lines.

items.title: <span>
items.text:
An inline container.

<p>
    This is <span>one</span> sentence.
</p>

The <span> stays within the surrounding line of text.

items.title: Grouping with Classes and IDs
items.text:
These elements are often given class or id attributes so that they can be identified.

<div class="card">
    <h2>Python</h2>
    <p>A programming language.</p>
</div>

A class can be used to identify multiple elements that belong to the same category.

<section class="course">
    <h2>Python Course</h2>
</section>

<section class="course">
    <h2>HTML Course</h2>
</section>

An id identifies a particular element.

<div id="main-content">
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
</div>

Classes and IDs are particularly useful when working with CSS and JavaScript.

items.title: Combining the Elements
items.text:
A webpage can use all three elements together.

<section>

    <h2>Our Courses</h2>

    <div class="course">
        <h3>HTML</h3>
        <p>Learn how to build <span>web pages</span>.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="course">
        <h3>Python</h3>
        <p>Learn how to build <span>programs</span>.</p>
    </div>

</section>

Here:

  • <section> represents the Courses section.
  • <div> groups each individual course.
  • <span> identifies a small piece of text within a paragraph.

items.title: Choosing the Right Element
items.text: When grouping content, ask what the group means.

items.title: Use <section> when:
items.text:
The content represents a distinct thematic section.

<section>
    <h2>Our Services</h2>
    ...
</section>

items.title: Use <div> when:
items.text:
You need a generic container and there is no more meaningful semantic element.

<div>
    ...
</div>

items.title: Use <span> when:
items.text:
You need to group or identify a small inline piece of content.

<p>This is <span>important</span> information.</p>

items.title: Important Elements
items.text: Element Purpose <section> Groups thematically related content <div> Generic block-level container <span> Generic inline container class Identifies one or more elements as belonging to a group id Gives an element a unique identifier

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Remember the difference:

<section>
    A meaningful section of the document
</section>

<div>
    A generic block-level group
</div>

<p>
    Some text with a
    <span>small inline group</span>
    inside it.
</p>

A useful way to think about them is:

<section> = meaningful group

<div> = generic block group

<span> = generic inline group

items.title: 18 - Page Landmarks: header, nav, main, footer, article, aside
items.text:
Goal: Learn how to divide a web page into meaningful areas using semantic HTML elements.

HTML provides several elements that describe the role of different parts of a page.

Instead of using <div> for everything, we can use elements such as <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> to tell browsers, search engines, screen readers, and other tools what each part of the page represents.

items.title: A typical page structure
items.text:
A simple web page might look like this:

<body>

    <header>
        <h1>My Website</h1>
    </header>

    <nav>
        <a href="index.html">Home</a>
        <a href="about.html">About</a>
        <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
    </nav>

    <main>

        <article>
            <h2>Learning HTML</h2>
            <p>HTML is used to structure web pages.</p>
        </article>

        <aside>
            <h2>Related Topics</h2>
            <p>Learn about CSS and JavaScript next.</p>
        </aside>

    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>Copyright 2026 My Website</p>
    </footer>

</body>

The important idea is that each element tells us what the content is for, not just how it should look.

items.title: <header>
items.text:
The <header> element contains introductory content for a page or a section.

<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
    <p>Learn web development</p>
</header>

A page header might contain:

  • A website logo
  • The website name
  • A heading
  • Introductory information
  • Navigation

For example:

<header>
    <h1>Uganda Travel Guide</h1>
    <p>Discover places to visit in Uganda.</p>
</header>

items.title: Important
items.text:
<header> does not necessarily mean the very top of the entire page.

It can also be used inside another semantic element.

<article>

    <header>
        <h2>10 Places to Visit in Uganda</h2>
        <p>Published on October 1, 2026</p>
    </header>

    <p>Uganda has many interesting places to visit...</p>

</article>

Here, the <header> belongs to the <article>.

items.title: <nav>
items.text:
The <nav> element contains important navigation links.

<nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="about.html">About</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

It is commonly used for:

  • Main website navigation
  • Section navigation
  • A table of contents
  • Other major groups of navigation links

For example:

<nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="courses.html">Courses</a>
    <a href="projects.html">Projects</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

items.title: <nav> does not mean every link
items.text:
Not every group of links needs to be inside <nav>.

For example:

<p>
    Read our <a href="privacy.html">privacy policy</a>.
</p>

This does not need a <nav> element.

Use <nav> when the links form an important navigation area.

items.title: <main>
items.text:
The <main> element contains the main content of the page.

<main>
    <h1>Learning HTML</h1>

    <p>
        HTML is the language used to structure web pages.
    </p>
</main>

A typical page might have:

<body>

    <header>
        <h1>My Website</h1>
    </header>

    <nav>
        <a href="/">Home</a>
        <a href="/about.html">About</a>
    </nav>

    <main>
        <h2>Welcome</h2>
        <p>This is the main content.</p>
    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>Copyright 2026</p>
    </footer>

</body>

items.title: Important rule
items.text:
A page should normally have one <main> element representing the primary content.

Content that appears repeatedly across pages, such as navigation or a site footer, generally does not belong inside <main>.

items.title: <footer>
items.text:
The <footer> element contains information about the page or a section.

A page footer might contain:

  • Copyright information
  • Contact information
  • Links
  • Author information
  • Related information

Example:

<footer>
    <p>Copyright 2026 My Website</p>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact us</a>
</footer>

Like <header>, a <footer> can belong to the whole page or to a specific section.

For example:

<article>

    <h2>Learning HTML</h2>

    <p>HTML gives structure to web pages.</p>

    <footer>
        <p>Written by Jonathan</p>
    </footer>

</article>

Here, the footer belongs to the article rather than the entire website.

items.title: <article>
items.text:
The <article> element represents a self-contained piece of content.

The content should make sense on its own and could potentially be distributed or reused separately.

Examples include:

  • A blog post
  • A news article
  • A forum post
  • A product review
  • A comment
  • A social media post

Example:

<article>
    <h2>What is HTML?</h2>

    <p>
        HTML is a markup language used to structure
        content on the web.
    </p>
</article>

A page can contain multiple articles:

<main>

    <h1>Latest News</h1>

    <article>
        <h2>New School Opens in Kampala</h2>
        <p>The school opened this week...</p>
    </article>

    <article>
        <h2>Local Students Win Competition</h2>
        <p>The students won the competition...</p>
    </article>

</main>

Each <article> represents a separate piece of content.

items.title: <aside>
items.text:
The <aside> element contains content that is related to the surrounding content but is not part of its main flow.

It is commonly used for:

  • Sidebars
  • Related articles
  • Author information
  • Advertisements
  • Additional information
  • Related links

Example:

<aside>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>

    <a href="css.html">Learn CSS</a>
    <a href="javascript.html">Learn JavaScript</a>
</aside>

Another example:

<article>
    <h1>Learning HTML</h1>

    <p>
        HTML is used to structure content on the web.
    </p>

    <aside>
        <h2>Did you know?</h2>
        <p>HTML was first introduced in the early 1990s.</p>
    </aside>
</article>

The information in the <aside> is related to the article but is not part of its main content.

items.title: Putting everything together
items.text:
Here is a more complete page:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">

<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My Blog</title>
</head>

<body>

    <header>
        <h1>My Blog</h1>
        <p>Thoughts about technology and programming.</p>
    </header>

    <nav>
        <a href="index.html">Home</a>
        <a href="articles.html">Articles</a>
        <a href="about.html">About</a>
    </nav>

    <main>

        <article>

            <header>
                <h2>Why I Like Python</h2>
                <p>Published on October 1, 2026</p>
            </header>

            <p>
                Python is a programming language known for its
                readable syntax and large ecosystem.
            </p>

            <p>
                It can be used for web development, automation,
                data analysis, and many other tasks.
            </p>

            <footer>
                <p>Written by Jonathan</p>
            </footer>

        </article>

        <aside>
            <h2>Related Articles</h2>

            <a href="fastapi.html">Introduction to FastAPI</a>
            <a href="django.html">Introduction to Django</a>
        </aside>

    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>Copyright 2026 My Blog</p>
    </footer>

</body>

</html>

Notice that the page has two different kinds of headers and footers:

Page
├── header
│   └── Website introduction
│
├── nav
│   └── Main navigation
│
├── main
│   ├── article
│   │   ├── header
│   │   ├── article content
│   │   └── footer
│   │
│   └── aside
│
└── footer
    └── Website footer

The inner <header> and <footer> belong to the <article>, while the outer ones belong to the page.

items.title: Semantic HTML vs <div>
items.text:
You could technically build the same page using <div> elements:

<div>
    <div>
        <h1>My Blog</h1>
    </div>

    <div>
        <a href="/">Home</a>
        <a href="/articles.html">Articles</a>
    </div>

    <div>
        <div>
            <h2>My Article</h2>
            <p>Article content...</p>
        </div>

        <div>
            <h2>Related</h2>
            <p>Related information...</p>
        </div>
    </div>

    <div>
        <p>Copyright 2026</p>
    </div>
</div>

The browser can display this, but the HTML does not clearly communicate what each part means.

Compare:

<div>
    <h1>My Blog</h1>
</div>

with:

<header>
    <h1>My Blog</h1>
</header>

The second version communicates that this is a header.

This is the purpose of semantic HTML.

items.title: <header>
items.text:
Use for introductory content belonging to a page or section.

<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
</header>

items.title: <nav>
items.text:
Use for an important group of navigation links.

<nav>
    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about.html">About</a>
</nav>

items.title: <main>
items.text:
Use for the primary content of the page.

<main>
    <h1>About Us</h1>
    <p>We teach programming.</p>
</main>

items.title: <article>
items.text:
Use for content that represents a self-contained piece.

<article>
    <h2>My Blog Post</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</article>

items.title: <aside>
items.text:
Use for related or supplementary content.

<aside>
    <h2>Related</h2>
    <p>More information...</p>
</aside>

items.title: <footer>
items.text:
Use for footer information belonging to a page or section.

<footer>
    <p>Copyright 2026</p>
</footer>

items.title: The difference between <section> and <article>
items.text:
These two elements are often confused.

A <section> groups content that belongs to a particular theme or part of a page.

An <article> represents a self-contained piece of content.

For example:

<main>

    <section>
        <h2>Latest Articles</h2>

        <article>
            <h3>Learning Python</h3>
            <p>Python is...</p>
        </article>

        <article>
            <h3>Learning HTML</h3>
            <p>HTML is...</p>
        </article>

    </section>

</main>

Here:

  • <section> groups the latest articles.
  • Each <article> is an independent piece of content.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
1. Use semantic elements when they accurately describe your content.
  2. Use <main> for the primary content of the page.
  3. Use <nav> for important navigation areas.
  4. Use <article> for self-contained content.
  5. Use <aside> for related or supplementary content.
  6. <header> and <footer> can belong to the whole page or to individual sections and articles.
  7. Do not use these elements simply because they have a particular visual appearance.
  8. Use CSS to control how semantic elements look.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Element Purpose <header> Introductory content for a page or section <nav> Important navigation links <main> Main content of the page <article> Self-contained piece of content <aside> Related or supplementary content <footer> Footer information for a page or section

The main idea is:

<header>   → What introduces this page or section?
<nav>      → Where can I navigate?
<main>     → What is the primary content?
<article>  → What is a self-contained piece?
<aside>    → What is related but secondary?
<footer>   → What information belongs at the end?

These elements give your HTML meaning and structure, rather than just grouping elements together.
